Abstract,"ZY-Path is a local PyQt5 desktop application for model-aware histopathology classification, combining Single image and Tiled analysis modes, spatial inspection, SQLite history, recorded rerun and export, with a separate supervisor-provided segmentation integration. On 7,180 CRC-VAL-HE-7K patches, the classifier achieved 90.68% accuracy and 88.59% macro-F1 through both the recorded OpenCV/Albumentations pipeline and the application’s default Pillow Single image core, with agreement on all predicted labels. The complete native Windows automated suite passed all 370 tests; UAT, segmentation accuracy, systematic performance measurement and clean-machine deployment remain to be evaluated.","Deploying pathology models through separate scripts makes preprocessing, spatial sampling and previous analysis settings difficult to inspect. This project develops ZY-Path, a local PyQt5 desktop application that connects supported PyTorch CPU inference to explicit Single image and Tiled analysis controls, spatial inspection, recorded history and export, with a separate supervisor-provided segmentation integration. The classifier achieved 90.68% accuracy and 88.59% macro-F1 on 7,180 native 224 × 224 CRC-VAL-HE-7K patches through the application’s default Pillow core, agreeing with every predicted label from the recorded reference pipeline. The 19 October Windows baseline passed 370 automated tests. The engineering contribution is a model-aware desktop workflow with explicit crop geometry, independent task semantics and reproducible parameter restoration. UAT, final-version manual Windows acceptance, systematic performance measurements and clean-machine deployment remain incomplete.",Update current implementation details while reporting only the dated Windows execution and preserving uncollected evidence as pending.

The evaluation consequences are discussed in Section 4.5.3.,"Source crop dimensions determine the field of view before resampling to 224 × 224. At the source dataset’s nominal 0.5 μm/pixel, a 224-pixel edge spans 112 μm. If a new raster’s resolution r is known in μm/pixel, a candidate crop edge covering that field is approximately 112/r pixels; this is a physical-scale calculation, not evidence of optimal predictive performance.
